summary:
On Mars, the strongest solar storm Curiosity has measured peaked 53 minutes after it began, and a message to Earth and back takes up to 44 minutes. When something goes wrong during a Marswalk, astronauts are on their own. NASA lists this as a problem it has not yet solved (Civil Space Shortfalls, 2026).

Solway is an incident-response system for astronauts on the Martian surface. It watches for dangers like solar storms and marsquakes and finds the safest way to shelter in seconds.

It shows each danger on a live 3D map of the real terrain, built from NASA data: HiRISE and CTX elevation models, Curiosity radiation and weather, and InSight marsquakes. Before suggesting a route, it tests it with a thousand virtual astronauts to see where a crew could fail. The crew gets one clear answer: where to go, how long it takes, how much oxygen will be left and which dangers the route avoids. It also plans science walks in Melas Chasma, such as a trip to a freshly fallen boulder.

The live web app runs in any browser: storm and quake drills from any point, a 3D map, a simulated helmet display with turn-by-turn guidance, and any place on Mars with a NASA elevation model.
details:
Solway: one answer when every minute counts

Solway is an incident-response system for astronauts walking on Mars. When something goes wrong, it detects the incident and shows it on a live map and a 3D view of the real terrain. It updates the dangers around the crew: steep slopes, rockfall zones, loose sand, radiation and places with no radio contact.

What it does

  • Finds every route to shelter and tests each one with a thousand virtual astronauts who get tired, overheat, use oxygen and can fall.
  • Stress-tests its own routes, searching for the most likely way each one can fail.
  • Gives the crew one clear answer: where to go, how long it takes, how much oxygen will be left and which dangers the route avoids.
  • Guides the crew turn by turn in a simulated helmet display: the route drawn on the ground ahead, the countdown against the 30-minute shelter rule, and oxygen, heat and dose against their limits.

New: the live web app

Runs in any browser, with no server and no install.

  • Storm and quake drills from any point you click on the map
  • Plan a walk between any two points
  • 3D map and helmet display of the route
  • Anywhere on Mars: pick any point and Solway loads the best NASA elevation model there and grades it as EVA-grade (HiRISE), route-planning grade (CTX) or not suitable for a walk. The global map shows all 1,216 HiRISE elevation models.

Our demo also plays three linked incidents: a solar storm based on the 20 May 2024 event, a marsquake that sets off rockfalls, and a science trip to a freshly fallen boulder.

Why it matters

The main benefit is time. A message to Earth and back takes up to 44 minutes, while the strongest solar storm Curiosity has measured peaked in 53. Solway answers in seconds and works fully offline.

Every number on screen is labelled as measured, modelled, assumed or scripted, with its source, so the crew knows what to trust. The same screen works on a laptop, a tablet or a wrist display.

NASA lists on-site support for spacewalk dangers on Mars as an open need (Civil Space Shortfalls 2026, item 8.06). Solway is a working prototype of that tool. Today it can help mission planners compare sites and plan safer walks; later, it could travel with the crew. The same approach could help teams on Earth that work far from help, such as polar field crews or mountain rescue.

How we built it

  • Engine: Python (numpy, numba, FastAPI), PyTorch for the stress test and the walking policy of the virtual astronauts
  • Dashboard: Electron, React, Tailwind, Recharts
  • Live web app: TypeScript, React, three.js, Web Workers, hosted on Vercel
  • 3D view and video: Unreal Engine 5.8

Data

  • HiRISE and CTX terrain from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter
  • Radiation and weather from Curiosity
  • InSight marsquake catalogue
  • JPL Horizons
  • NASA DONKI space weather records
  • ESA Mars Climate Database dust conditions (Space Agency Partner data)

What makes it different

The map reacts. It does not just show where danger is; it decides where to walk and shows why, by trying to break its own routes before the crew uses them. It also turns danger into opportunity: a fresh boulder brings down rock from cliffs nobody can climb, the same reason Apollo 17 sampled the boulders at Station 6.

Choices and limits

  • Crew safety first: a 30-minute shelter rule and suit limits for heat, oxygen and slope taken from NASA spacewalk studies.
  • A real site: Melas Chasma in Valles Marineris, one of the three front-runners at NASA’s 2015 Human Landing Sites workshop, in a canyon system shown in 2026 to be tectonically active.
  • The decision first on screen, for moments of stress.
  • Honest limits: scripted incidents, results from our own models, no tests with a crew; the helmet display is a simulation, not AR hardware.

Use of AI

Narration, music and sound effects in the demo video were generated with ElevenLabs. Code was written with the help of an AI coding assistant. The 3D shots are real-time renders of NASA terrain in Unreal Engine 5; no AI-generated images or video are used.
